lesson.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV
lesson.goal: load a CSV with pandas, then select, filter, clean and group the data

sources.title: Learn Pandas in 30 Minutes - Load, Select, Filter, Clean and Group a CSV

steps.title: Install pandas and load CSV
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `uv init .` and `uv add pandas` (or `pip install pandas`), download orders.csv from https://github.com/techwithtim/PanadasTutorial, and create main.py that imports pandas as pd, reads orders.csv with pd.read_csv and prints df. Run `uv run main.py` and see the rows x columns summary.

targets.caption: Import pandas with the conventional pd alias
Load orders.csv into a DataFrame
The printed DataFrame ends with its rows x columns summary

explanations.topic: Installing pandas with pip / pip3
Using a uv virtual environment (uv init, uv add, uv run)
Why import pandas as pd
DataFrame vs Series
CSV and two-dimensional data
read_csv stores the file in a DataFrame
Reading the printed table (40 rows x 9 columns)

hints: Install pandas first: `uv add pandas` in a uv project, or `pip install pandas` (`pip3` on Mac/Linux).
Put orders.csv in the same folder as main.py so the relative path 'orders.csv' resolves.
main.py needs three lines: `import pandas as pd`, `df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')`, `print(df)`.
Run it with `uv run main.py` (or `python main.py`) and look for '[40 rows x 9 columns]' at the bottom of the output.
common_mistakes: Running `python main.py` outside the uv venv after `uv add pandas`, giving ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas'.
orders.csv not in the working directory, causing FileNotFoundError.
Typo `pd.readcsv` or `pd.read_CSV` instead of `pd.read_csv`.
Saving the GitHub HTML page instead of the raw CSV, so the file doesn't parse as expected.
Forgetting `print(df)`, so nothing appears when running a .py file.
steps.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')
print(df)

steps.title: Load data in Jupyter notebook
steps.instructions: Create notebook.ipynb (Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+P → New Jupyter Notebook); in cell 1 import pandas as pd and load orders.csv with pd.read_csv, then print df in cell 2.

targets.caption: First cell: import pandas and load the CSV
Second cell: print the DataFrame
Printed DataFrame output under the cell

explanations.topic: Why use a Jupyter notebook instead of a plain .py file for pandas
Creating a notebook with Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P → New Jupyter Notebook
Installing the VS Code Python extension for notebook support
Cells can be run independently; data stays loaded between cells
Running, deleting cells and clearing outputs

hints: Open the command palette (Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+P), choose 'New Jupyter Notebook', and save it as notebook.ipynb in the folder that contains your CSV.
In the first cell, import pandas as pd and assign df = pd.read_csv('your_file.csv'), then run the cell and choose a Python kernel.
Add a second cell below with print(df) and run only that cell. df is still in memory from the first cell.
If you see ModuleNotFoundError, select the kernel/interpreter where pandas is installed. If you see FileNotFoundError, check that the CSV is in the same folder as the notebook.
common_mistakes: Saving the notebook outside the folder containing orders.csv, causing FileNotFoundError
Selecting a kernel/Python interpreter that doesn't have pandas installed (ModuleNotFoundError)
Running the print cell before the read_csv cell, giving NameError: name 'df' is not defined
Not having the VS Code Python/Jupyter extension, so 'New Jupyter Notebook' doesn't appear
Saving the file with a .py extension instead of .ipynb
steps.run_command: Run cell 1 (pick a Python kernel), then run cell 2 in the Jupyter notebook
steps.code:
# cell 1
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('orders.csv')

# cell 2
print(df)

steps.title: Explore the DataFrame
steps.instructions: In main.ipynb run df.head(), df.tail(), df.info() and df.describe() in cells. Then inspect df.columns and df.index.

targets.caption: Preview the first five rows
Column names, non-null counts and dtypes
Descriptive statistics for numeric columns
RangeIndex: start, stop, step

explanations.topic: head() shows the first five rows instead of the whole DataFrame
tail() shows the last five rows
info() gives entry count, columns and dtypes
Why text columns show as object instead of string
describe() generates descriptive statistics such as quartiles
df.columns lists column names; df.index is a RangeIndex

hints: Make sure the cell that loads your CSV into df has been run first, then add new cells below it.
Methods need parentheses: df.head(), df.tail(), df.info(), df.describe().
columns and index are attributes, not methods: write df.columns and df.index with no parentheses.
If nothing prints, put each expression as the last line of its own cell, or wrap it in print().
common_mistakes: Running the cells before the cell that defines df, which causes a NameError.
Writing df.columns() or df.index(), which raises a TypeError because these are attributes, not methods.
Leaving off the parentheses on df.head, which shows a bound method instead of the table.
Putting several expressions in one cell, so only the last one's output is displayed.
Expecting describe() to summarise text columns by default; it only covers numeric columns unless include='all' is passed.
steps.run_command: Run each cell in the Jupyter notebook (Shift+Enter)
steps.code:
df.head()
df.tail()
df.info()
df.describe()
df.columns
df.index

steps.title: Select columns and rows
steps.instructions: In main.ipynb select one column with df['col'] and several with df[['col1', 'col2']]. Select rows by position with df.iloc[0] and df.iloc[10]['col'].

targets.caption: Select one column, which returns a Series
Select several columns, which returns a DataFrame
Pick a row by position, then read a value by column name

explanations.topic: Indexing a column returns a pandas Series
Using len() and set() on a Series
Passing a list of columns returns a DataFrame instead of a Series
iloc selects rows by integer position
A row can be indexed by position or by column name; pandas types differ from Python types

hints: Look at df.columns first so you know the exact column names.
One column uses single brackets: df['ColumnName']. Several columns need a list inside the brackets: df[['A', 'B']].
Rows by position use iloc: df.iloc[0] gives the first row.
Chain the two to get one value: df.iloc[10]['ColumnName'].
common_mistakes: Using single brackets with several names, e.g. df['Country', 'Product'], which raises a KeyError. You need double brackets.
Misspelling or using the wrong case for a column name (e.g. 'country' instead of 'Country'), which raises a KeyError.
Writing df.iloc(0) with parentheses instead of square brackets.
Asking iloc for a row past the end, e.g. 40 in a 40-row frame, which raises an IndexError.
Expecting a Series from a multi-column selection. Two or more columns return a DataFrame.
steps.code:
df.columns
df['Country']
len(df['Country'])
set(df['Country'])
df[['Country', 'Product']]
df.iloc[0]
df.iloc[10]
list(df.iloc[10])
df.iloc[10][0]
df.iloc[10][1]
df.iloc[10]['Country']

steps.title: Filter with boolean conditions
steps.instructions: In main.ipynb filter rows with df[df['col'] == value], combine conditions with & and | in parentheses, and filter numerically, e.g. df[df['Quantity'] > 2].

targets.caption: Filter rows where a column equals a value
Combine conditions with & (and) or | (or), each in parentheses
Numeric comparison filter

explanations.topic: Boolean mask: df[df['col'] == value] keeps matching rows
An empty table can mean the condition was put on the wrong column
Use a single & for 'and' with each condition in parentheses
Use a single | for 'or'
Numeric comparisons >, <, <=, != as filters

hints: Inside df[...], put a condition such as df['SomeColumn'] == 'SomeValue'.
To combine two conditions, wrap each one in parentheses and join them with & for and, or | for or.
Numeric columns work the same way: df[df['Quantity'] > 2].
If you get an empty table, check that the value actually appears in the column you're filtering, including its case.
common_mistakes: Filtering the wrong column (e.g. Product instead of Category) and getting an empty result
Using Python's `and`/`or` instead of `&`/`|`, which raises a ValueError about ambiguous truth value
Forgetting parentheses around each condition when combining with & or |
Case mismatch in the string value (e.g. 'electronics' vs 'Electronics')
Comparing a numeric column to a string like '2'
steps.code:
df[df['Category'] == 'Electronics']
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') & (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[(df['Category'] == 'Electronics') | (df['Country'] == 'USA')]
df[df['Quantity'] > 20]
df[df['Quantity'] > 2]
df[df['Quantity'] <= 2]
df[df['Quantity'] != 2]

steps.title: Use string and isin filters
steps.instructions: In your notebook, filter names with `df[df['CustomerName'].str.startswith('A')]` and `.str.endswith('a')`. Use `df[df['Country'].isin([...])]` and negate it with `~`.

targets.caption: Filter rows by the start of a string column
Filter rows by the end of a string (case-sensitive)
Keep rows whose value is in a list
Tilde reverses the isin condition

explanations.topic: Using the .str accessor for string methods on a column
String matching is case-sensitive (endswith('A') finds nothing)
isin replaces a long combined OR condition
The ~ operator negates a boolean condition in pandas

hints: Wrap a boolean condition in df[...] to keep only matching rows, just as in the previous step.
String methods live under .str: df['YourColumn'].str.startswith('A').
For several allowed values, use df['Country'].isin([...]) with a list.
Put ~ in front of the condition, ~df['Country'].isin([...]), to get everything NOT in the list.
common_mistakes: Calling df['CustomerName'].startswith('A') without .str, which raises AttributeError.
Using the wrong case, e.g. endswith('A') instead of 'a', and getting an empty result.
Passing values to isin separately instead of as one list: isin('USA','Sweden').
Using not or ! instead of ~ to negate the condition.
Misspelling the column name (e.g. 'Customer Name'), which raises a KeyError.

steps.title: Update data with loc
steps.instructions: Change values with `df.loc[condition, 'Column'] = value`, e.g. set Country USA to 'United States'. Uppercase a column with `df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()`.

targets.caption: Locate the rows by a condition, then assign to a column
Uppercase a whole column

explanations.topic: loc locates rows by label or condition, unlike iloc, which uses the index position
loc returns a DataFrame because several rows can match
Use row condition, column then = value to update the matching cells
Replacing every USA value with United States
Reassigning a column with .str.upper()

hints: Start with df.loc[condition] alone to check which rows match.
Add a comma and a column name inside the brackets, then assign a value with =.
For the whole column, write df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper().
Check the column names with df.columns. In this dataset the column is 'Product', not 'ProductName'.
common_mistakes: Using df.iloc with a boolean condition instead of df.loc.
Writing df[df['Country']=='USA']['Country'] = ..., which is chained assignment and does not update df.
Calling df['Country'].upper() without .str.
Running .str.upper() without assigning the result back to df['Country'].
Misspelling a column name, which causes a KeyError or silently creates a new column.
steps.code:
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...', 'Product'] = 'Tim'
df.loc[df['CustomerName'] == 'Anna ...']
df.loc[df['Country'] == 'USA', 'Country'] = 'United States'
df[df['Country'] == 'USA']
df[df['Country'] == 'United States']
df['Country'] = df['Country'].str.upper()
df['Country']

steps.title: Drop rows and clean data
steps.instructions: Remove a row with `df = df.drop(<index>)` and check `df.tail()`, then reload the CSV. Use `df.dropna()`, `fillna(...)` and `df.rename(columns={...}, inplace=True)`.

targets.caption: Drop a row by its index label
Remove rows with missing values
Modify the DataFrame in place
Rename a column

explanations.topic: drop removes a row by index label
dropna drops rows containing null/NA values
fillna replaces missing values instead of removing
inplace=True modifies vs returns a new DataFrame
Renaming columns with rename

hints: df.drop(label) returns a new DataFrame, so assign it back: df = df.drop(39).
Check df.tail() afterwards. The dropped index should be gone. Re-run pd.read_csv to restore the data.
For missing values try df.dropna(), or df['Col'].fillna(0, inplace=True).
Rename with df.rename(columns={'Old': 'New'}, inplace=True), then display df.
common_mistakes: Calling df.drop(39) without assigning or inplace=True, so the row is not removed.
Dropping an index label that doesn't exist (KeyError) because the row was already dropped on a rerun.
Expecting df.dropna() to change df without assigning the result.
Misspelling the column name in fillna or rename, which raises a KeyError or silently renames nothing.
Forgetting to reload the CSV before continuing, so later steps use modified data.
steps.code:
df = df.drop(39)
df.tail()

# reload the CSV
df = pd.read_csv('data.csv')

df.dropna()

df['OrderID'].fillna(0, inplace=True)

df.rename(columns={'OrderID': 'Order ID'}, inplace=True)
df

steps.title: Analyze, group and save
steps.instructions: In notebook.ipynb, run value_counts(), a groupby(...)[...].sum() and sort_values(..., ascending=False) on your DataFrame. Save it with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False).

targets.caption: Count how often each value appears
Group rows and sum a column
Sort rows, highest first
Save the cleaned DataFrame to a new CSV

explanations.topic: value_counts gives a count of each unique value in a column
groupby works like SQL GROUP BY: aggregate a column per group
sort_values with ascending=False sorts descending
to_csv index=True/False controls whether the index is written

hints: Call value_counts() on a single column, e.g. df['Country'].value_counts().
For groupby: pick the grouping column, then select the column to aggregate and call .sum(): df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum().
sort_values takes the column name and ascending=False for highest first.
Save with df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False) and check the file appears in the file browser.
common_mistakes: Calling df.value_counts() on the whole DataFrame instead of one column.
Writing df.groupby('Country').sum() without selecting Price, which sums every numeric column or errors on text columns.
Using ascending='False' (a string) or forgetting ascending=False, so results sort low to high.
Typing df.2csv or df.toCSV instead of df.to_csv.
Omitting index=False, so the saved CSV gets an extra unnamed index column.
Price column still stored as text from earlier cleaning, so sum concatenates strings instead of adding.
steps.code:
df['Country'].value_counts()

df.groupby('Country')['Price'].sum()

df.sort_values('Price', ascending=False)

df.to_csv('new_file.csv', index=False)
